subject: biology
title: Enzymes and the lock-and-key model
key_idea: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They speed up reactions in living things without being used up. Each enzyme has an active site with a shape that fits only its own substrate, which is explained by the lock-and-key model.

blocks.text: Reactions in living cells would be far too slow without enzymes. This section covers what enzymes are and what they do.

items.meaning: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up.
A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up reactions in living organisms.
The molecule that an enzyme acts on.
The molecule or molecules made in the reaction.
The part of the enzyme where the substrate binds.

items: Enzymes are made of protein, which is made of amino acids.
Each enzyme catalyses one specific reaction, because of the shape of its active site.
Enzymes break large molecules down, as in digestion. They also build large molecules up from small ones.
Carbohydrases, proteases and lipases are enzymes that break down carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
An enzyme is a biological catalyst. It speeds up a reaction and is not used up.
Enzymes are proteins.
Each enzyme catalyses a specific reaction.

blocks.text: The lock-and-key model explains how an enzyme works. The substrate is the key and the active site is the lock.

diagram.alt: Put the stages of the lock-and-key model in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the lock-and-key stages in order
steps: The substrate binds to the active site because their shapes are complementary
The reaction happens and the substrate is broken down into products
The enzyme is unchanged and can be used again

blocks.text: Complementary means the shapes fit together exactly. They are not the same shape.

items: Each enzyme has an active site with one particular shape.
Only a substrate with a complementary shape fits into the active site.
A substrate with the wrong shape cannot bind, so no reaction takes place.
For example, amylase breaks down starch. It cannot break down protein, because protein does not fit its active site.
The substrate fits the active site because their shapes are complementary.
The substrate is broken down and the products are released. The enzyme is not used up.
A different substrate does not fit, so the enzyme is specific.

blocks.text: Exam questions use the model to explain why an enzyme will or will not work. Always name the active site and the substrate.

rows: How does amylase break down starch?
Starch binds to the active site. The shapes are complementary. Bonds are broken to give smaller molecules.
Why will urease not break down starch?
Enzymes are specific. Starch does not fit the active site, so no reaction takes place.
What happens when an enzyme gets too hot?
It is denatured. The shape of the active site changes (covered in the next note).

items: Say the substrate binds to the active site. Saying it only "fits" is ignored in some answers.
Use the words complementary, specific and active site.

checks.a: A biological catalyst, which speeds up reactions in living organisms. It is a protein.

checks.q: Why does each type of lipase act on only one type of lipid molecule?
checks.a: Each active site has a specific shape, so only one type of lipid molecule fits.

checks.q: Explain how amylase breaks down starch, in terms of the lock-and-key model.
checks.a: Starch binds to the active site, because the shape of the active site and the starch are complementary. A reaction occurs, breaking the bonds between the starch molecules to produce smaller molecules.

worked_example.question:
Amylase is an enzyme that breaks down starch.

Explain how amylase breaks down starch.

Answer in terms of the 'lock and key theory'.
answer_points: Starch (the substrate) binds to the active site.
Because the shape of the active site and the shape of the substrate are complementary.
A chemical reaction occurs to produce smaller molecules, or the bonds between the starch molecules are broken to produce smaller molecules (allow maltose or sugars).
worked_example.tip: Three separate marks. Saying that the starch fits the active site does not score the first mark. Say that it binds.

worked_example.question:
Urease is an enzyme that breaks down urea into smaller molecules.

Explain why urease will not break down starch into smaller molecules.
answer_points: Enzymes are specific.
Their shape is complementary to their substrate.
So starch will not fit into the active site (of urease).
So no reaction can take place.
worked_example.tip: Any three of the four points score one mark each. Write them as a linked chain.

worked_example.question:
Explain why the enzyme amylase cannot break down the substrate protein.

Include ideas about the active site.
answer_points: Enzymes are specific.
The active site has a particular shape, which is complementary to the substrate.
Only starch will fit or bind into the active site of amylase.
Protein will not fit or bind into the active site.
Enzyme-substrate complexes cannot form.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score one mark each. Mentioning lock and key is allowed. Saying the enzyme is denatured loses the active site shape, fit and complex points.

worked_example.question: Explain why lipase cannot be used to catalyse the breakdown of proteins.
answer_points: Enzymes are specific.
The only substrate for lipase is fat (lipid) molecules.
The shape of the active site is complementary to fat, not to protein.
Protein cannot fit into or bind to the active site of lipase.
Enzyme-substrate complexes cannot form.
worked_example.tip: Any three of these points score the marks.

blocks.text: Metabolic reactions are the chemical reactions that keep an organism alive. Enzymes are involved in all of them.

items: Without enzymes these reactions would be too slow to sustain life at body temperature.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an **enzyme-substrate complex**.
The substrate is changed into products, which leave the active site. The enzyme is unchanged.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Specificity depends on the complementary shape and fit of the active site with the substrate.

items: **Pectinase** breaks down pectin in fruit cell walls. This gives more juice and a clearer juice.
(Supplement) **Lactase** changes lactose into glucose and galactose. This makes lactose-free milk.

worked_example.question:
In some countries, snails are farmed as a source of protein. A scientist investigates the effect of temperature on the growth of snails.
The scientist measures the mean shell height of groups of snails kept at three different temperatures for 24 weeks.

Time in weeks | Mean shell height in mm at 8 °C | at 15 °C | at 23 °C
0 | 15.0 | 15.0 | 15.0
8 | 15.2 | 15.8 | 17.0
16 | 15.5 | 16.8 | 20.4
24 | 16.4 | 18.2 | 21.8

Explain the effect of temperature on the growth of snails in this investigation.
answer_points: Higher temperatures produce more growth.
Enzymes are involved.
More kinetic energy.
More frequent collisions, so enzyme-substrate complexes form faster.
Faster respiration.
worked_example.tip: Any three of these points score the marks.
